This page records the preliminary extension plan for the Publishing and AI Checkpoint. The extension has not yet been fitted or independently verified.

## Starting point

**AI system and date:** OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex, November 6, 2026.

Our question is how NBA team statistics predict regular-season winning percentage. Our course-based baseline is simple linear regression of winning percentage on field-goal percentage, both measured on a 0–100 scale. Across 715 team-seasons with year labels 2000–2023, the estimated slope is approximately 5.10 percentage points of winning percentage per one-percentage-point higher field-goal percentage (conventional 95% confidence interval: 4.54–5.65). The in-sample R-squared is approximately 31.4%.

The baseline omits defense and assumes a straight-line relationship. We want to investigate whether nonlinear relationships and interactions improve prediction while retaining regression as the core of our case study.

## Substantive prompts

Akira submitted this exact extension-selection prompt:

> Our STAT 330 project asks how NBA team statistics predict regular-season winning percentage. Our baseline is simple linear regression predicting winning percentage from field-goal percentage, both on a 0–100 scale. Across 715 team-seasons from 2000–2023, the slope is about 5.10, with a 95% confidence interval of 4.54–5.65, and R-squared is 31.4%.

> The baseline omits defense and assumes a linear relationship. Suggest three feasible beyond-course extensions, including decision-tree regression and Gaussian process regression. Explain how each would strengthen this same research question, how its results would enter our final case study, and two independent ways to verify it. Keep our regression analysis central and do not choose for us.

The AI suggested decision-tree regression, Gaussian process regression, and random-forest regression, with proposed applications and verification checks. Akira selected decision-tree regression. No extension implementation prompts have been used yet.

## My decisions

- **Accepted:** Propose a decision-tree regression comparator that can capture thresholds and interactions among shooting and defensive statistics. We plan to use R's `rpart` package with a continuous response and `method = "anova"`.
- **Changed:** We will compare the tree not only with the field-goal-percentage baseline, but also with a course-based regression using the same predictors and observations. This helps distinguish gains from added defensive information from gains due to changing the model form. Candidate variables include field-goal percentage, points per game, turnovers, rebounds, and defensive rating, subject to data checks.
- **Not selected:** Gaussian process regression and random forests are outside the scope of the selected extension. They are alternatives, not methods shown to be unsuitable by our results.
- **Evaluation plan:** Reserve later complete seasons as a test set. Tune tree complexity and prune using only earlier training seasons, keeping seasons together during resampling. Evaluate all comparators on the identical test observations using RMSE in winning-percentage points. Exclude wins, losses, winning percentage, and variables calculated from wins or losses from the predictor set.

**Connection to the final case study:** We plan to report the tree's method, main splits, and comparison with regression in the "A new direction with AI" section of the case-study page. Its purpose is to investigate whether thresholds and interactions improve the same prediction task. The course-based regression and two required course-method families will remain central. No improvement is claimed before evaluation.

## Independent verification

These are two planned checks, not completed verification results.

1. **Documentation and manual calculation:** Check the regression settings, complexity controls, and pruning behavior against the official [`rpart` documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/rpart/html/rpart.html). After fitting an unweighted regression tree, manually route selected training rows through the split rules and confirm that the prediction in a terminal node equals the mean winning percentage of its training observations. Record the calculation and whether it matches the package output.
2. **Held-out comparison and error calculation:** Compare the pruned tree with the baseline and a same-predictor course-based regression on later seasons excluded from training and tuning. Independently calculate RMSE as `sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2))` from the saved test predictions and compare it with the reported evaluation output. Record the errors and whether any improvement is consistent across additional season-based validation splits within the training period.

Another AI response will not be treated as an independent check. Results and supporting evidence will be added after implementation.

## Remaining limitation

A single tree may be unstable: small changes in the training seasons can change its splits. Tree-based associations do not establish causality. Because predictors summarize the same season as the outcome, test results would measure prediction using completed-season statistics, not preseason forecasting ability. Changing NBA conditions and repeated franchises may also limit generalization.
